EU Imposes 200-Day Import Quotas on Hybrid Vehicles Produced in China, Japan, UK, US, and More
29 photos
Photo: MG
As expected, the European Union has decided on limiting imports of new hybrid passenger cars from a bunch of major exporting countries. The quota system will go into effect on December 1, 2026, and run through June 18, 2027, introducing a 200-day safeguard that covers full hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and mild hybrids.
Regulation 2026/2614 clearly states that additional qualifying vehicles from a given country are prohibited from entering the European bloc once an individual quota runs out. The union's trade measure affects China, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States, Turkey, South Korea, Mexico, Morocco, South Africa, Serbia, and other countries.
Only 822 vehicles are listed under the 'other countries' quota, but more curiously, South Africa is listed as 'not applicable'. On closer inspection, South Africa is omitted from Annex I.2, which lists developing countries that exceed the 3 percent EU hybrid import threshold.
In other words, South African-built hybrids are exempt for the time being from the provisional safeguard that European legislators designed to protect European automakers. Brussels introduced this safeguard as a response to rising imports from outside the bloc, imports that are often more affordable than European hybrids.
The European Commission points to falling domestic market share and deteriorating profitability as well, which is crazy when you remember that hybrid vehicles are increasingly popular across the European space. If you ask me, high prices and pitiful quality both hinder European automakers right now.
There's also the matter of high energy costs and high labor costs, of course, but on the ground, it's hard to make a case for the shoddy interior plastics and the poor after-sales service of many European automakers. China gets the largest piece of the pie, with Japan not far behind. For all countries, the Commission has divided the restriction into three separate periods.
Photo: MG These run from December 1, 2026, through February 28, 2027, then March 1 through May 31, and June 1 through June 18. All told, China received a total allowance of 191,780 hybrids across those 200 days. Japan got 170,899 vehicles, while Turkey received 126,320 across all three periods. The United Kingdom and South Korea got 105,402 and 67,924 vehicles.
Mexico couldn't do better than 34,755 vehicles, Morocco 23,954, Serbia 19,353, and the United States 18,482. Combined, total allocations amount to 759,681 vehicles for the entire 200-day period. Each country-specific quota is based on 2025 import volumes, adding slightly more than 15 percent.
Countries that accounted for more than 2 percent of European hybrid imports during 2025 received individual allocations. Unused quantities are to carry over in the following period, thus preventing manufacturers from losing access to an allocation because they didn't make the best of the initial three-month period.
Per regulation 2026/2614, customs authorities determine the hybrid vehicle's origin under the EU's non-preferential origin rules. This, in turn, makes the actual production location and applicable origin criteria extremely important. Chinese exporters, which pose the biggest threat to Europe's automotive industry, face an additional requirement.
Importers seeking access to China's allocation must present a signed and stamped export quota certificate issued by the CCCME, namely the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products. Otherwise put, the CCCME is in total control of dividing up the hard cap of 191,780 Chinese-built hybrids .
Via // EUR-Lex
